import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 457

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/457](https://www.erdosproblems.com/457)
-/

namespace Erdos457

/--
Is there some $\epsilon > 0$ such that there are infinitely
many $n$ where all primes $p \le (2 + \epsilon) \log n$ divide
$$
  \prod_{1 \le i \le \log n} (n + i)?
$$

This was formalized in Lean by Baretto and van Doorn using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/main/ErdosProblem457.lean"]
theorem erdos_457 : answer(True) ↔ ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ),
    { (n : ℕ) | ∀ (p : ℕ), p ≤ (2 + ε) * Real.log n → p.Prime →
      p ∣ ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊Real.log n⌋₊, (n + i) }.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- Let $q(n, k)$ denote the least prime which does not divide
$\prod_{1 \le i \le k}(n + i)$. -/
noncomputable abbrev q (n : ℕ) (k : ℝ) : ℕ :=
    Nat.find (Nat.exists_prime_not_dvd (n := ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊k⌋₊, (n + i))
      (Finset.prod_ne_zero_iff.2 fun a ha => by aesop))

/--
More generally, let $q(n, k)$ denote the least prime which
does not divide $\prod_{1 \le i \le k}(n + i)$. This
problem asks whether $q(n, \log n) \ge (2 + \epsilon) \log n$
infinitely often.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_457.variants.qnk : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ),
    { (n : ℕ) | (2 + ε) * Real.log n ≤ q n (Real.log n) }.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
Taking $n$ to be the product of primes
between $\log n$ and $(2 + o(1)) \log n$ gives an example where
$$
  q(n, \log n) \ge (2 + o(1)) \log n.
$$
Can one prove that $q(n, \log n) < (1 - \epsilon) (\log n)^2$
for all large $n$ and some $\epsilon > 0$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_457.variants.one_sub : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ),
    ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, q n (Real.log n) < (1 - ε) * Real.log n ^ 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos457

findings.description: The construction in the opening docstring (lines 60–64) has an indexing slip; the theorem itself is correct. Since `q n k` uses the factors n+1,…,n+⌊k⌋, a prime p dividing n with ⌊k⌋ < p divides none of those factors, so q(n,k) ≤ p. Thus taking n itself to be the indicated product of primes leaves a missing prime near log n, rather than giving the claimed lower bound near 2 log n. The general implication `p.Prime → p ∣ n → ⌊k⌋₊ < p → q n k ≤ p` was proved in the scratch file.
findings.source_evidence: This typo is inherited from the source's commentary. Terence Tao explicitly corrects it in https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/457#post-4665 (7 March 2026): the construction needs the product over i=0,…,k−1 rather than i=1,…,k to work literally. The upper-bound question itself is stated correctly at https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/1181.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the definition of `q` and the theorem unchanged. Omit the ancillary construction sentence, or explain the necessary one-step shift: with the current indexing, take n+1, rather than n, to be the prime product.

status_issues.evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/457 says “This has been solved in the affirmative and the proof verified in Lean.” In https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/457#post-4648, Thomas Bloom records on 7 March 2026 that the upper-bound question was separated as Problem 1181 and Problem 457 marked solved. reformulations.difference: Uses q(n,log n) ≥ (2+ε)log n instead of requiring every prime p ≤ (2+ε)log n to divide the product. Pointwise, the latter corresponds to a strict lower bound on q.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For any real cutoff x, all primes p ≤ x divide the product iff x < q, by q's minimality and nondivisibility. Consequently the main statement implies the q variant with the same ε. Conversely, a witness ε>0 for the q variant gives the divisibility statement with ε/2: for n>1, (2+ε/2)log n < (2+ε)log n ≤ q. The cases n=0,1 are harmless; indeed their divisibility predicates hold. Proved the complete equivalence as `Review457.main_iff_q_variant` in /workspace/review/scratch.lean, without sorryAx.
